title: The Fundamental Group
notes: Open by making the fundamental group feel like a measuring instrument for path failure. A loop is not just a curve returning home; after endpoint-fixed homotopy, it becomes a word, a relation, a covering action, or a tree pattern. Point out the assigned source span so students know this deck is the chapter map rather than a replacement for the text.

title: Endpoint-Fixed Homotopy
notes: Use the endpoint pins as the first invariant the class should protect. Homotopy is allowed to move the middle of the path, but the endpoints stay fixed for every time value. Then tie the basepoint join to the loop product: the product is a loop only because the first loop ends exactly where the second one starts.

title: The Group Law
notes: Treat the group law as a construction that survives deformation. Concatenation gives multiplication, the constant loop gives the identity, and reversing time gives inverses. The important caution is that products live at a chosen basepoint, so the operation is not just a rule for arbitrary closed curves floating in the space.

title: Basepoints Matter
notes: This is the place to slow down on basepoints. Changing basepoints by a path h transports loop classes by conjugation, which explains why unbased loop information loses a chosen representative and keeps only conjugacy. The notebook check verifies that this transport respects products, so the formula is not merely a mnemonic.

title: The Circle
notes: For the circle, emphasize unwrapping. A loop on S1 returns to the same visible point, but its lift to the real line can end at a different integer. That endpoint is the winding number, and the artifact checks windings from minus one through three, all projecting back to the same basepoint downstairs.

title: Maps Induce Homomorphisms
notes: Maps of spaces become maps of groups by sending each loop through the continuous map. The diagram artifact packages three moves students will reuse constantly: functorial composition, product splitting, and the retraction argument for injectivity. Use the torus pair and circle degree checks as quick computational witnesses.

title: Free Product Words
notes: Reduced words prepare the algebraic side of van Kampen. The free product keeps track of which piece each segment came from before any commutativity is imposed. Walk through the cancellation table as a finite model: only adjacent inverse letters cancel, and the notebook check distinguishes ab from ba.

title: van Kampen Statement
notes: State van Kampen as assembly with a quotient. The free product records local loops in the cover pieces, while the normal subgroup forces overlap loops to agree after entering the whole space. The connected nerve and triple-intersection check are there to keep the hypotheses visible instead of hidden in prose.

title: van Kampen Proof Moves
notes: The proof moves are the theorem in action: subdivide a loop so each small part sits in one cover set, replace those parts by local loop data, then compare alternative decompositions by overlap relations. Stress why normal closure appears: a relation may be carried around by paths before it is killed.

title: Attaching 2-Cells
notes: A 2-cell is best understood as a relation-maker. Its boundary word becomes nullhomotopic after the disk is attached, so the fundamental group is quotiented by the normal closure of that word. The abelianization checks provide sanity tests: genus two orientable rank four, and nonorientable genus three carrying Z over 2 torsion.

title: Torus-Knot Presentations
notes: Use the torus-knot slide as a compact presentation example. The geometry supplies two natural generators, and van Kampen supplies the single relation a to the m equals b to the n. Abelianization is not the full group, but the rank-one check is a useful quick test for the coprime examples.

title: Covering Spaces
notes: Covering spaces turn local sameness into global bookkeeping. In graph covers of a wedge of two circles, the fiber over the basepoint is a set of sheets, and each generator lifts as a permutation of those sheets. The gallery shows that connectedness can be read as a single orbit.

title: Monodromy
notes: Monodromy is the action version of lifting. A loop at the basepoint moves a chosen sheet to another sheet, giving a permutation of the fiber. When the generated action is transitive, the cover is connected. Compare the regular four-sheet example with the nonnormal three-sheet example to separate transitivity from regularity.

title: Classification
notes: Classification reverses the arrows students may expect. Subgroups of the fundamental group classify connected covers, with smaller subgroups giving larger covers. A covering map downward corresponds to subgroup inclusion upward. The lattice artifact makes this reversal concrete and records a directed acyclic organization with the universal cover at the top.

title: Deck Transformations
notes: Deck transformations are the symmetries of the cover that sit over the identity map downstairs. For the cover associated to a subgroup H, the deck group is the normalizer quotient N of H over H. Normal subgroups give regular covers, and the checks contrast deck order four with the nonnormal order-one case.

title: Graphs Are Free
notes: Graphs are the most visible free groups in the chapter. Choose a maximal tree, collapse it, and every chord becomes one free generator. The numerical check E minus V plus one equals four gives students a fast way to test the picture while remembering that the basis depends on the tree.

title: K(G,1) And Bass-Serre
notes: The K(G,1) and Bass-Serre slide points beyond the chapter without leaving its logic. A K(G,1) has all higher homotopy suppressed, so the fundamental group becomes the main homotopy invariant. Bass-Serre theory then organizes group splittings by universal covers that look like trees; the artifact is a finite tree window.

title: Instructor Exercise: Build A Cover From Permutations
notes: Close with an instructor exercise that uses the applied lab data rather than a new theorem. Ask students to compute orbits and decide regularity from the two permutations. Then reveal the sanity checks: one orbit, monodromy group of order one hundred twenty, deck symmetry order one, and a connected but nonregular cover.
